analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and payroll taxes on high earners to keep the program solvent.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; no vote was ever scheduled before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would boost Social Security benefits in several ways: it raises the replacement rate for lower earners, increases benefits for people who draw them for 20 years or past age 82, raises the minimum benefit toward the poverty line based on years worked, credits unpaid family caregivers with deemed wages, eliminates the five-month disability waiting period, and switches cost-of-living adjustments to an index that tracks prices seniors actually pay. To pay for it, the bill would progressively phase out the payroll tax cap above $142,800 — fully taxing all wages by 2026 — and raise the net investment income tax on investment gains from 3.8% to 6.8%.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners, the very old, long-term disabled applicants, unpaid family caregivers, and low-income retirees — plus the program's future solvency, since new revenue extends the trust funds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the factor applied to the first tier of earnings in the benefit formula from 90% to 95%, lifting benefits for lower earners, and counts a share of earnings above the old tax cap so higher-taxed workers also earn credit [S3].
Adds a 5% benefit increase for anyone who has drawn benefits for 240 months or reaches age 82, helping the oldest retirees who outlive their savings [S3].
Creates a new minimum benefit that rises with years worked, reaching 125% of the poverty guideline for someone with 30 or more years of work, aimed at lifetime low earners [S3].

Credits unpaid caregivers of young or chronically dependent relatives with deemed wages worth 50% to 100% of the national average wage, so time out of the workforce for care work no longer zeroes out their benefits [S3].
Eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits and surviving-spouse benefits, so disabled workers and widows get paid from the first month of eligibility [S3].
Switches cost-of-living adjustments to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, reflecting the medical-heavy spending of retirees rather than the general index [S3].
Protects SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries from losing means-tested benefits when their higher Social Security checks arrive [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners: workers and self-employed people earning above the current payroll tax cap would be taxed on wages above it (starting at 80% in 2022 and reaching all wages by 2026), and high-income households would pay 6.8% instead of 3.8% on net investment income [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill is a large tax increase on high earners: wages above the cap would go from untaxed to fully subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax, and the investment-income tax rate rises 3 points, which supporters would have to defend openly [S3].

The caregiver-credit program relies on self-certification and applications to the Social Security Administration for care that is hard to verify, which is why the bill requires the Commissioner to write anti-fraud regulations — an administrative burden and a program open to disputes about eligibility [S3].

Only 44.1% of the higher investment-income tax goes to the Social Security trust fund, with the remainder continuing to fund Medicare and general revenue, so the solvency math depends on provisions spread across programs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and concrete — bigger checks for low earners, the old, the disabled, and caregivers, funded by dedicated new revenue rather than borrowing, which would also extend the trust funds. The cost is concentrated and real: a phased-in full removal of the payroll tax cap and a higher tax on investment income for the top of the income distribution. The honest trade-off is a large, broad public benefit paid for by a narrow, well-off group; the design is straightforward even where the caregiver-credit verification is awkward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Schatz introduced the bill on October 26, 2021, with Sen. Duckworth joining, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee that same day [S5].
That referral was the last action of record; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and one other Democratic senator cosponsored over the bill's lifetime [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and investors who would have paid the new payroll and investment-income taxes are better off because the bill never moved; Social Security beneficiaries are not, since the benefit increases never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who would have paid the new taxes

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill expanding Social Security benefits and funding them with payroll-tax and investment-income tax increases.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Joined Schatz in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred and never taken up
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 26, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship and the single cosponsor were all Democratic, with no Republican support of record, and the bill died in committee with no recorded opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill phases out the $142,800 payroll tax cap until all wages are taxed, hitting the top slice of earners with the full 12.4% Social Security tax on income they currently pay it on only up to the cap.
The net investment income tax on capital gains and other investment income rises from 3.8% to 6.8%, a direct increase in the tax cost of investment returns for higher-income households.
